# Locale review

<!-- Generated by tools/i18n/build-locale-review.mjs. Do not edit by hand. -->

The interface is offered in 14 languages. English is the source. The other 13 are **AI-generated drafts** written by the same AI that built this app. No native speaker has reviewed any of them. Each screen in those languages shows a label saying so, and every disclaimer is shown with its English text (content-safety rule 3, decisions-log section G).

## How a language loses the AI label

A named human reviewer and an ISO review date in the `_meta` of the locale file. Nothing else removes it.

## Automated checks every locale passes

Same keys as English. Same `{placeholders}`. Every number in the English line appears with the same value (digits of other scripts are read as numbers). No empty text.
These terms stay as written: `Language Lab`, `USCIS`, `N-400`, `DHS`, `uscis.gov`, `A-number`.
Nothing may equal the English text except: `app.name`, `report.take`, `stage.n400_interview.short`, `stage.civics.short`, `settings.textSize.normal`.
The checks do not read meaning. That is what the sheets are for.

## Choices to confirm

- **Chinese is Traditional** (`zh-Hant`, shown as 中文（繁體）). It follows USCIS's Chinese materials. Simplified Chinese is not provided.
- **Filipino** uses the language tag `fil`. Haitian Creole is shown as Kreyòl ayisyen. Hmong is White Hmong (RPA spelling).
- **Home heading.** In every language the home heading is "Welcome to Language Lab" (not the English "Welcome to the booth"), and the word "booth" in the home lead is rendered as a quiet room or space. English still says "booth". This was decided for Vietnamese in step 5 and applied to the others to match.
- **Tagalog** shows "Sibika (Civics)" for three labels that would otherwise equal the English.
- **Dates** use the Gregorian calendar and Latin digits in every language. Where the browser has no data for the language (Hmong, Haitian Creole in current browsers), month names are English.

## Back-translation pass

I translated the disclaimer, privacy and legal lines (16 keys, 13 languages) back into English and compared them with the source. This is a weak check: the same AI wrote the drafts and read them back. The back-translations are in each sheet, first section.

### Found and fixed

- ru `lang.interviewEnglish`: "unless USCIS allows" was written as "if USCIS does not allow" (reads as the opposite). Rewritten in two sentences.
- ru `partReport.scope`: "how you would do on the real test" was written as "how you would have passed the real test" (implies pass/fail). Changed to "how you would perform".
- tl `partReport.scope`: "how this part went" was written as "how this part succeeded" (nagtagumpay), and the real-test clause was clumsy. Rewritten.
- lo `aiNotice.text`: "authoritative" was written as "has power" (ມີອໍານາດ). Changed to "used as the main one".
- hmn `aiNotice.text`: "authoritative" was written as "has power" (muaj hwjchim). Changed to "official", as in translation.notice.
- my `aiNotice.text`: "authoritative" was written as "has power" (အာဏာရှိ). Changed to "official".
- ru, lo, th, ko, hi, pt `aiNotice.text`: "Authoritative" was rendered as "main", "standard", "authentic" or "the one that counts". All six now say "official", as translation.notice does.
- hmn `header.about, home.full.text, compare.setting`: Named in the audit (CON-02): "About us and warning", "according to cutting" (used twice). Rewritten as "About Language Lab and the disclaimer", "one part after another", "one word after another". Not reviewed by a Hmong speaker.

### Still differs a little

- hmn `aiNotice.text`: "authoritative" is rendered as "official" (raug cai): close, slightly weaker.
- hmn `intro.privacy`: "fictional profile" is rendered as "made-up model" (tus qauv tsim los). The word qauv (pattern, model) may not be the natural word for a profile. Needs a Hmong reader.
- hmn `n400.sample.note`: Same word (qauv) for the made-up profile.
- hmn `help.setup.2`: Same word (qauv) for the profiles.
- hmn `intro.profile.legend`: Same word (qauv) for "profile".
- hmn `intro.profile.help`: Same word (qauv) for "profile".
- hmn `common.fictional`: Same word (qauv) for "profile".
- hmn `header.about`: "Txog peb thiab ceeb toom" reads as "About us and warning", not "About & disclaimer". Needs a Hmong reader.
- hmn `compare.setting`: "in order" now "ib lo tom qab ib lo" (one word after another) and "may be missing" "poob tau" (may fall out). Still needs a Hmong reader.
- hmn `voice.consent.text`: "Say" is the plain verb for speaking, and "language" (lus) stands in for "words". Needs a Hmong reader.
- hmn `compare.setting.writing`: "punctuation" is rendered as "stopping marks" (cov cim nres) and "spelling" as "writing". Needs a Hmong reader.
- hmn `coach.notice.text`: "fictional" is "not real" and "on/off" is "open/closed" (qhib, kaw). Needs a Hmong reader.
- hmn `coach.privacy`: "salted code" is rendered as "secret number" (lej zais). Needs a Hmong reader.
- my `aiNotice.text`: "authoritative" is rendered as "official": close, slightly weaker.
- my `compare.notYet`: "Not yet" is rendered literally as "has not arrived yet". Low confidence.
- my `voice.consent.text`: "voice recording system" for "voice recognition" (အသံမှတ်သားစနစ်): recording and recognition are not the same thing. Needs a Burmese reader.
- my `coach.notice.text`: "fictional" is "imaginary" (စိတ်ကူးယဉ်). Needs a Burmese reader.
- tl `aiNotice.text`: "authoritative" is rendered as "valid" (may bisa): close, slightly weaker.
- ko `compare.counts`: "This counts" is rendered "is accepted" (인정됩니다), a little stronger than "counts".
- ko `intro.locked`: "Answer key" is rendered "answer table" (정답표); fine in context.
- th `civics.officialNote`: "Any one of these answers counts" is rendered "counts as correct" (นับว่าถูก), slightly stronger.
- th `report.lead.onTrack`: "civics" is rendered as "civic duties" (หน้าที่พลเมือง), as elsewhere in the Thai file.
- lo `civics.officialNote`: Same: "counts as correct" (ນັບວ່າຖືກ).
- ru `compare.setting.writing`: "counted as correct" (засчитываются) is a little stronger than "still count". Close enough; a Russian reader should confirm.

### Confidence

Least confident: Hmong (hmn), Lao (lo), Burmese (my), Haitian Creole (ht). Then Thai (th), Filipino (tl), Hindi (hi). I have no confidence figure for the rest: the back-translation pass found real meaning errors in Russian and Filipino too. This is my own estimate from vocabulary range and the amount of stiff phrasing I found, not a measurement.

Burmese: the font stack is for Unicode Burmese. Phones that still use Zawgyi-encoded text may show garbled letters; this has not been tested.
